Deep reddish orange is the sixth and last of the oranges in Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's color nomenclature, a burnt, earthy orange defined by its goldfish, apple and topaz.

Deep royal blue is exactly what its name describes: a darker-than-usual variant of [[royal-blue|royal blue]], built by the same "intensity plus base color" grammar as most of ColorHub's modifier names.

Deep Saffron is a strong, warm orange named for the dye and spice taken from crocus stigmas, and our archive's earliest match for it predates the color's own written record by nearly four centuries, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin.
Deep Sky Blue is a vivid, light azure from the X11 color list, with sky blue as its parent entry in Paterson.
Deep Slate-Blue is a dark, muted blue named for slate stone, recorded in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, carried into the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, and most over-represented in paintings from India.
Deep Slate-Violet is a muted purple-grey, filed by our library as a slate word rather than a violet one.
Deep teal green is a dark, blue-leaning green, a shade down from plain [[teal]].
Deep Terracotta is a dark, burnt orange-red close to the fired clay it is named for, and close to a hue Werner's 1821 nomenclature of colours called "Tile Red".
Deep Turtle Green is a muted, yellow-leaning green, named for the animal rather than a plant.
Deep Vinaceous-Lavender is a dusty, wine-tinted lavender, Ridgway's reading of a muted purplish grey.
Del Monte is a muted grey-violet from the 1930 Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and the books say nothing about where the name came from.
Delft blue is named after the blue-and-white pottery of Delft in Holland, Europe's answer to Chinese porcelain; as a color name it has drifted from the pottery's bright cobalt to a soft, greyed blue.
Delphinium is a color named for the tall blue garden flower, a name that the chart-makers kept even after the swatch grew greyer than the petals.
Denim is the mid-blue of indigo-dyed cotton twill, the cloth of blue jeans; its name probably comes from a French town, though the books agree on little else about where the word began.
Desert Sand is a pale, warm, pinkish tan, the color of dry dunes in a crayon box and in the ISCC-NBS list; the books that mention desert sand more often call it red.
Diamin-Azo Blue is a dark, greyed purple-blue from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, a shade close enough to the library's Independence that the two are only a few points apart.
Dijon is a mustard-toned yellow-green named for a Burgundy city; the color books are silent on it, but the city shows up in them for a different reason, as the place where zinc white was worked out.
Dim Grey is a neutral mid-dark grey from the X11 color list, exactly 105 on each of red, green and blue.
Dirty Pink is a muted, slightly brownish rose first recorded by the 2010 xkcd color survey, where volunteers typed names at swatches on screen.
Dirty Yellow is a dense, greenish yellow named by the 2010 xkcd color survey, and one of the rarest colors we can match in painting.
Diva Blue is a strong purplish blue recorded on both Ridgway's 1912 chart and in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, with no book in our library explaining the theatrical name.
Dodger Blue is a bright, saturated azure from the X11 color list, one of the web's standard blues.
Doe is a light, warm tan from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the female deer, and one of the most common colors in our entire painting archive.
Dove grey is the soft plumage color of the dove, and the books disagree on whether it leans blue, pink or purple.
Drabolve is a dull, dark yellow-olive from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, filed by later standards as a moderate olive.
Dragon's Blood is a brick red, catalogued by our library as a plant word and first recorded in print in 1599.
Duck green is the dark green of a mallard's neck and of yew leaves in the old naturalists' color charts, and also, confusingly, the name of a pale green in later dictionaries.
Dull Blue is a muted, mid-toned slate blue named by the 2010 xkcd color survey, common enough to turn up in a Monet sunset and a Fra Angelico Madonna alike.
Dull Brown is a descriptive name, not a pigment or a place: a brown with the brightness taken out, which the color books mention only in passing.
Dull Dark Purple is a muted, reddish purple first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, and nearly identical to the crowd-named Dirty Purple a century on.
Dull Green is a plain descriptive name for a mid green of low saturation, and as a painters' word it means a green with its chroma turned down.
Dull Lavender is a pale, greyed pinkish lilac, the sort of color that sits on the edge between a purple and a neutral.
Dull Magenta Purple is a muted reddish purple plotted on Ridgway's 1912 color atlas and later absorbed into the ISCC-NBS dictionary as a moderate reddish purple.
Dull Opaline Green is a very pale, slightly grayed green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, closer to celadon porcelain than to any garden green.
Dull Orange is a muted, earthy orange, a descriptive name more than a historical one.
Dull Purple is a muted reddish purple; the name is a plain modifier, and the books use the phrase for puce and for what happens when painters mix red, yellow and blue.
Dull Red is a descriptive name, a red with the shine taken out, and the books use it as a plain adjective phrase more than as the name of any one dye or pigment.
Dull Teal is a greyed, muted [[teal]], recorded in both Wikipedia's color list and the 2010 xkcd survey.
Dull yellow is a plain description rather than a historic name: a yellow with its brightness turned down, the kind of yellow that weld, buckthorn lake and ochre gave painters.
Dusk Blue is a deep, slightly greenish blue that our library finds under three other names within two units of distance.
Dusk is the dim time after sunset, and as a color it is a muted blue-violet, a dark with a little blue left in it.
Dusky Blue is a dark, greyed [[blue]] with three separate sources on file, from Ridgway's 1912 plates to the 2010 xkcd survey.
Dusky Green is a dusky shade of [[green|green]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

Livid Purple is a dusky, muted purple from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, one of the rarest colors in our painting archive, though a matching hue turns up in a Bronzino portrait painted 367 years before the name existed.
Dusky Orient Blue is a dark, greenish blue plotted in Ridgway's 1912 atlas and later carried into the ISCC-NBS dictionary, close to the blue called petrol.
Dusky Pink is a muted, slightly bluish rose, a long-running name for pinks that have lost their brightness.
Dusky plum is a dark, muted reddish purple, the 2010 xkcd survey's shaded take on the fruit color [[plum]].
Dusky Purplish Grey is a dark, near-neutral grey, built by stacking the modifiers dusky and purplish onto the base color grey rather than naming anything in particular.
Dusky Rose is a muted, slightly brownish pink, built by putting the modifier dusky in front of the base color rose rather than naming anything in particular.
Dusky Slate-Blue is a dark, muted blue-grey that our library finds almost identical to plain Charcoal.
Dusky Violet is a dim, greyed blue-violet, built by putting the modifier dusky in front of the base color violet rather than naming anything in particular.
Dusky Yellowish Green is a dim, greyed olive green, built by stacking the modifiers dusky and yellowish onto the base color green rather than naming anything in particular.
Dust is a dull greyish yellow-brown, the colour of dry earth on a surface, and the clearest case of the word in colour history is khaki, which means dusty.
Dusty Blue is a soft, greyed mid blue, a descriptive name that fits the faded look of old indigo work clothes.
Dusty cornflower is a muted, greyed blue, the library's softened variant of [[cornflower]], the blue named for the flower's petals.
Dusty crimson is a muted brick red, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Chōshun-iro, whose characters read literally as "long spring color."
Dusty Green is a mid green softened with grey, a plain descriptive name that appears in several color standards without a story of its own.
Dusty Grey is a middle, nearly neutral grey, built by putting the modifier dusty in front of the base color grey rather than naming anything in particular.
Dusty hazel tone is a dull yellow-green, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Koke-iro, literally "moss color."
Dusty hazel is a muted olive-brown, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Kimirucha, "yellow sea-pine brown."
Dusty hunter green is a muted, dark green, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Tokusa-iro, "horsetail color," after the horsetail plant.
Dusty khaki is a pale, greyed yellow-green, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Urahayanagi, "the underside of willow leaves."
Dusty Lavender is a pale, greyed purple close to the real flower [[lavender]], listed in the ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary as well as the 2010 xkcd survey.
Dusty marigold is a muted golden orange, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Kikuchiba, "golden fallen leaves."
Dusty maroon is a dark reddish brown, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Hihada-iro, "cypress bark color."
Dusty moss is a muted sage green, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Usu'ao, whose name literally means "pale blue."
Dusty Orange is a warm, slightly muted orange, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Beni'ukon, "red-bronze," literally red dye and turmeric.
Dusty oxblood is a dark reddish brown, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Tobi-iro, named for the kite, a bird of prey.
Dusty peach is a pale tan with a warm pink cast, ColorHub's English name for the Japanese traditional color Torinoko-iro, "eggshell paper color."
Dusty Pink is a muted, slightly bluish rose; the word *dusty* means a color with grey mixed in, and the name sits beside old rose and antique pink.
Dusty Plum is a dusty shade of [[plum|plum]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.
Dusty Purple is a muted, mid-dark [[purple]], carried by four separate sources on file, from the ISCC-NBS dictionary to a traditional Japanese name.
Dusty Red is a muted brick red that comes from the 2010 xkcd color-naming survey, where it was simply "dusty" put in front of [[red]].
Dusty rose brown is a muted, greyed pink-brown recorded by Werner in 1821, its name a plain description with no further story behind the choice of words.
Dusty Rose is a muted pink-red close to the color of a garnet, carried in the ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary and, almost a century and a half earlier, in Werner's 1821 nomenclature.
Dusty Teal is a mid-dark, muted [[teal]], recorded only by the 2010 xkcd crowd survey.
Saccardo's Violet is a soft, greyed violet from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color book, most likely named, like its sibling Saccardo's Slate, for the Italian mycologist Pier Andrea Saccardo.
Dutch Blue is a soft grey-blue, a name that has meant different things to dictionaries and to pigment makers.

Earth is the color of bare ground, a mid brown with an orange cast, and the name painters give to the oldest, cheapest and steadiest family of pigments: the ochres, siennas, umbers and green clays dug straight from the soil.
Easter Purple is a bright blue-violet from the 2010 xkcd color survey, close kin to lavender and ordinary purple, with no traceable coiner.
Ebony is the name of a dense tropical heartwood and, from it, of a glossy black; the swatch on screen is a dark green-grey, which is a good reason to read what the books say about the wood.
Ecru-Olive is a muted tan-olive that shares its ISCC-NBS block with at least ten other named colors.
Ecru is the pale warm off-white of cloth that has not been bleached or dyed, a French word that for centuries stood for what most white things really looked like.
Eggplant is a dark greyish purple named for the fruit of *Solanum melongena*, which British English calls the aubergine.
Eggshell Blue is a very pale, cool blue-green named for a bird's eggshell; as a screen swatch it reads as a minty near-white.
Eggshell Green is a pale, soft green, recorded by Maerz and Paul with a first-use date of about 1824.

Egyptian blue is a calcium copper silicate, fired from sand, lime and copper in Egypt some 4,500 years ago: among the oldest synthetic pigments, and the standard blue of the ancient Mediterranean for more than two thousand years.
Electric blue is a bright, saturated blue tied to the glow of electrical discharge; the name was in fashion shops by the 1870s, as a dusty periwinkle, long before it became the color of the future.

Emerald green is a brilliant cool green that began as the color of a gem and, from 1814, became the name of a copper-and-arsenic paint that colored Victorian wallpaper, Impressionist canvases and a famous poisoning rumor.
Emerald is a bright, slightly bluish green named after the gem, a beryl tinted by a trace of chromium, and it also names one of the most brilliant and most poisonous paints of the nineteenth century.
Emeraude is French for emerald, and as a color name it points less at the gem than at a green that French and English painters argued over.
Eminence is a deep purple, a dictionary name from the Maerz and Paul era whose meaning of rank and distinction is the only story our books support.
Empire Green is a dark, grey-leaning green tied to Napoleonic France, though Napoleon did not start the fashion.
English red is the old trade name for a red iron-oxide pigment, made by heating yellow ochre or iron sulfate, and it never meant one exact recipe or one place of making.
English Vermilion is a dulled, brick-leaning red from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, a quieter cousin of true vermilion, the bright red mercury-sulfide pigment.
Espresso is a very dark, reddish brown named for the coffee drink, close to black at a glance and warmer once it sits beside black.
Ether is a medium, slightly greenish blue recorded in the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930; no book we hold says who chose the name.
Ethereal Blue is a pale, slightly grayed sky blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1845 and closest to the core color sky blue.
Eton Blue is a school color: the light blue of Eton, a public school in England, whose name was later shared with a university.
Eucalyptus is a muted grey-green, named in a 1930 color dictionary for the tree.
Eupatorium Purple is a soft, greyed purple-pink carried into our library from a Japanese traditional color name, and it sits only 2.6 color-distance units from the common [[mauve]].
Evergreen is a dark forest green named for trees that keep their leaves, recorded in color dictionaries since 1915.
Faded Pink is a dusty, muted rose, built from the modifier "faded" laid onto ordinary pink rather than from any single dated source.
Faded Purple is ColorHub's name for Shion-iro (紫苑色), a traditional Japanese color named for the pale purple Tatarian aster flower.
Faded rosewood is a greyed, dusty red-brown, the library's washed-out variant of [[rosewood]], and it reads as a muted brick rather than as wood.

Faience is the glazed blue-green ceramic of ancient Egypt, a material that may have helped start glassmaking; the same word later named tin-glazed European earthenware, and a mid blue in a 1930 color dictionary.
Falcon is a dark brown, listed in a 1930 color dictionary under the name of the bird.
Fallen leaf is a dull gold-brown that our library also carries, at the identical hex, from a Japanese traditional color list.

Falu Red takes its name from the Falun copper mine in Sweden, whose iron-rich waste became the pigment behind the deep red barns of Scandinavia, and it is one of the most common reds in our entire archive.
Fandango is a strong reddish purple named for the Spanish dance, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary and still listed as an X11 web color today.
Fawn is the light brown of a young deer's coat, a name that sits in Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature and in a 1535 list of pleasing color pairs.
Fawn is a light yellowish brown named for the coat of a young deer, and Renaissance color writers had a lot to say about it.
Fern Green is a mid, slightly dulled green, dated by Maerz and Paul to 1902 and later adopted by RAL and Crayola.
Fern is a clear mid-bright leaf green, and an irony of dye history: ferns were among the plants northern Europeans used to dye green, yet gave weak, unstable results.
Ferruginous means rust-colored, from the Latin for rust, and describes the reddish brown of iron-bearing earths and stones.
Fibrous Green is a vivid yellow-green matched to RAL 6039, the German industrial color standard, not a traditional dictionary-of-color name.

Fiery Rose is a hot, saturated pink-red from Crayola's crayon list, close enough to Neon Fuchsia and Begonia Rose that only a careful eye tells them apart, and too bright for any painting in our archive to match.
Finn is a deep purple whose name has no documented origin in our sources; it is a color we can measure but cannot yet explain.
Fir Green is a dark, muted green whose name points to the fir tree, a descriptive name with no recorded inventor.
Fire Engine Red is a bright, vivid red, a descriptive name that points to the red of fire engines.
Flag is a dark, grayish purplish blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1918 and closest to navy among the core colors.

Flame Scarlet is a vivid reddish orange that Robert Ridgway carried over from his own 1886 color nomenclature into the 1912 standard, and that the ISCC-NBS system later filed under "vivid reddish orange."
Flame is a vivid reddish orange named for fire, though real flames are rarely this red, and in the pigment books the word names a black.
Flat Blue is an old dyer's grade of indigo, a middle-light blue on a ladder that ran from milk blue to navy, and also a Chinese name for the best azurite.
Flat Green is a muted, medium olive-green, named by the modifier "flat" the same way a paint chip is called flat rather than glossy.

Flax-Flower Blossom is a dusty, moderate blue named for the small sky-colored flowers of the flax plant, first recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1930 and distinguished from its closest neighbor by being a shade bluer.
Flax-flower blue is a soft, slightly purplish blue, number 30 among the blues of Werner's nomenclature of colors, where it is tied to a butterfly, the flax flower and a blue copper ore.
Flesh color is the old name for a warm, pale pink-orange, the shade painters and tailors once used for light skin.
Flesh Pink is a pale pinkish beige, a name from the old habit of describing colors by skin.
Flint Grey is a light, grayish yellowish brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, placed at the very start of their plate sequence with a first-recorded date of 1000.
Flirt is a deep purplish red, a name our library traces to the early twentieth-century color dictionaries rather than to any dye or flower.
Floral lavender is a brighter, more saturated purple than the muted [[lavender]] of the flower it is named for, and our painting archive has no record of it at all.
Floral White is a computer color name: one of the 140 colors in the X11 set, a white with a faint warm tint.
Folkstone is a light brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1928, its spelling a step away from the English town of Folkestone.
Fontainebleau is a light brownish grey, listed in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary under the name of the French royal court town and palace.
Forest green is a strong, mid-dark green named for woodland; as a screen color it is the web's ForestGreen, and the name itself was already in English use by 1810.
Forsythia is a moderate orange yellow named for the flowering shrub, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary and brighter than its archive namesake would suggest.
Foxglove is a medium purple named for the flower, though the books say more about the plant's role in green dyeing.
France Rose is a medium rose pink with a purple cast, known from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, where it is printed on plate 1.
Freedom is a deep blue with a slight violet lean, a color name from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary that no book in our shelf discusses as a color.
French Beige is a light-brown shade-name, one of a long run of "French" colors in the dictionaries, with no recorded story of its own.
French Blue is a strong blue with three histories: the blue of France's royal arms and flag, a name for artificial ultramarine, and a famous stolen diamond.
French green is a muted, slightly yellowish green that the dictionaries file under a country adjective, and that the paint trade used for an altogether different thing.
French grey is a pale, almost neutral grey that English first met as a naturalist's term: Patrick Syme put it on his 1814 color chart, and a young Charles Darwin used it for an octopus.
French White is a pale, greyish pink-lilac in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, and also an older name from the paint trade for a fine lead white.
Frostbite is a hot, bluish pink, a Crayola-list name whose swatch has little to do with the medical condition it is named for.
Fulvous is an old word for a dull orange or reddish-yellow, used above all for animal colors, especially bird plumage.
Fuzzy Wuzzy is a warm, reddish brown whose playful, reduplicated name has no documented origin in our sources, even though the color itself turns out to be common in old paintings.
Gamboge is the bright, slightly lemony yellow of a Southeast Asian tree resin, named for Cambodia, a watercolor of the East India trade and, in 1908, part of the evidence that atoms exist.
Garland Green is a muted yellowish green that Maerz and Paul recorded in their 1930 color dictionary, and no other system in our library has repeated the name since.
Garnet Brown is a dark, reddish brown named for the gem rather than its namesake's usual red, close enough to our library's Ox-Blood Red to be a near-duplicate.
Generic Viridian is a blue-green standing in for the pigment family named viridian, Latin for green, without claiming to be any one maker's exact hue.
Genoa Blue is a muted greenish blue in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name points to Genoa, the port whose cloth gave the world the word jeans.
Gentian Blue is a strong purplish blue named for the gentian flower, listed by Ridgway in 1912 and the ISCC-NBS in 1955.
Ghost White is a computer color name from the X11 set: a white tipped faintly toward blue.
Glacier is a dark, greyish blue-violet that appears in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, whose origin the sources do not explain.
Glass Green is a pale, slightly yellow green first set down by Ridgway in 1912 and repeated independently in both the ISCC-NBS and Maerz and Paul dictionaries.
Gnaphalium Green is a soft, pale grey-green named for Gnaphalium, the everlasting or cudweed genus whose leaves carry that same dusty tone, and recorded by Ridgway in 1912.
Gold is the warm, bright yellow of the precious metal, the color that stood in for heaven on medieval altarpieces and for wealth everywhere else, and the one color a screen can only imitate.
Golden brown is a rich yellowy brown, a name Paterson links to hair and to the lichen called crottle.
Golden yellow is a descriptive name for a warm, bright yellow, and across the centuries it has been attached to pigments, dyes and chemicals that share little beyond the adjective.
Goldenrod is the strong, slightly mustardy yellow of the flower of that name, and today it is best known as one of the 140 named colors of the web.
Gooseberry is a dark reddish purple from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name is stranger than the fruit, since the common gooseberry colour name is a green.
Gotham Green is a dark, slightly blue-leaning green named for Gotham, the old nickname for New York City.
Grape Purple is a very deep reddish purple named for the fruit's skin, one of several grape-based names in our library that do not quite agree on a single shade.
Grape is a dark reddish purple named after the fruit, though the books agree that the color is richer than real grapes and that the pigment called grape black is not purple at all.
Grapefruit is a bright coral red, named for the fruit's flush; the books read say little about it, so its history is mostly the library's record.
Graphite Grey is a dark, slightly blue-tinged grey named for the soft carbon of pencils, a mineral that contains no lead.
Graphite violet is a mid-grey with a faint violet lean, one of ColorHub's own core names built as a violet-leaning variant of graphite.
Graphite is the dark metallic grey of the soft carbon mineral inside a pencil, long mistaken for lead and named for writing.
Grass Green is a green named for turf: a yellowish green that Werner's mineral color table fixed as number 54, and that screens now show far brighter than any historical swatch.
Grass is the green of a lawn in the sun, but the older color books meant a quieter green by the name, and painters struggled for centuries to make it at all.
Grebe is a dark, warm grey with a brownish cast, named for the plumage of the diving water bird.
Green Beige is a muted tan with a faint greenish cast, standardized by the German RAL system in 1927 as RAL 1000 and common enough in old paintings to show up in roughly one in nine.
Green-Blue is a descriptive name, not a story: the slot between green and blue on a painter's color wheel, a standard color name, and a label that three sources attach to three different colors.
Green Brown is a plain descriptive name for a dull olive-khaki; as a swatch it is RAL 8000, a paint standard, and the books say little about it as a color.
Green earth is a pale, greyish green clay pigment, a mixture of celadonite or glauconite, that painters dug from Cyprus to Verona and laid under flesh for two thousand years.
Green grey is a descriptive name for a muted green with a good deal of grey in it; it is not a pigment or a dye, and the books use the phrase for many different things.
Green Yellow is the electric yellow-green of the web keyword `greenyellow`, a name that sits on a border which older European color orders refused to draw: a yellow that leans toward green.

Green is the color of leaves and grass, everywhere in nature yet hard for people to make or keep: for centuries an unstable color of youth, love, chance and poison, and today the color of nature itself.
Greenish Black is one of the named blacks in Werner's nomenclature of colors, the mineralogist's vocabulary of the 1770s, and its swatch on a screen is a neutral dark grey with no green in it at all.

Greenish blue is a blue leaning toward green: an old descriptive phrase that Abraham Werner's mineral colors turned into a fixed name, and that dictionaries still use for everything from peacock feathers to a pale winter horizon.

Greenish bottle green is a deep, cool green carried into our library from the Japanese traditional color Aotake-iro, named for green bamboo, and it sits only 3.0 units from the plain [[bottle-green]].
Greenish Cyan is a vivid, minty blue-green, built from the modifier "greenish" on cyan rather than coined whole.
Greenish Grey is a grey with a faint green cast, a name from the mineralogists' color charts of the 1790s that Syme fixed as number 15 in his 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*.
Greenish hospital green is a pale, cool green, the library's bluer-leaning variant of the institutional [[hospital-green]], and it is rare enough in our archive that five matches stand out.
Greenish hunter green is ColorHub's name for Aoni (青丹), a traditional Japanese color whose name, "blue-black clay," reflects an older sense of *ao* spanning blue, green and grey.
Greenish Slate-Black is a very dark, greened grey named for the rock, slate, standing almost on top of Dark Slate Grey and Bluish Slate-Black in the ISCC-NBS system's 1955 list.
Greenish white is the sixth white in Werner's colour chart, a snow white with a trace of green, shown on a goldcrest's feathers, a narcissus petal and a lump of calc sinter.
Greenish yellow is a yellow tipped toward green, a color that Europeans have long found hard to like and that mineralogists, dyers and pigment makers have each had to name.

Grenadine Pink is a strong yellowish pink that Ridgway placed in his 1912 color nomenclature, later filed by the ISCC-NBS system alongside two dozen other trade names in the same small region of color space.

Grey aqua is a muted, greyed blue-green that our library carries as an English rendering of Mizu-iro, a traditional Japanese water color, close enough to Grey teal that only half a unit of greenness separates them.
Grey Beige is a light, greyed tan, the color of undyed wool and dry dust, named by blending two neutral words.
Grey Blue is a muted, slightly greenish sky blue, a plain name built from two colour words that most traditions have used for a very long time without ever fixing it to one pigment.
Grey brown is a name for a dull, warm neutral, and it has meant two quite different swatches: a mid olive-tinged brown on screens today and a near-black in older charts.

Grey celadon is a soft, muted green that takes its name from celadon ware, the pale jade-green glazed pottery of East Asia, and that our library carries as a rendering of the traditional Japanese Seiji-iro.
Grey green is a descriptive name for a muted green, best known in the books through celadon, the pale Chinese glaze, and through the way distance dulls foliage.
Grey Olive is a very dark, greyed olive, a name our library files under a Japanese traditional color and an early German standard.
Grey pink is a descriptive color name, a pink greyed down until it is dusty, and it has more to say about how we name colors than about any one history.
Grey Purple is a muted, dusty violet, a plain descriptive name that several color systems recorded long before screens did.

Grey teal is a muted, greyed blue-green named for the teal duck's head feathers, carried by Ridgway in 1912 and the ISCC-NBS system in 1955, and painted most often by Eugène Boudin among the artists in our archive.
Grey white is a pale warm off-white, and in our data a paint-industry name from the RAL system.

Grey is the color between black and white, the one color that is named after nothing; it has meant poverty, hope, old age and good taste in turn, and it changes its look more readily than any other color.
Greyish black is a black softened with grey, a name that appears as number 17 among the blacks in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of the mineralogist Werner's color list.
Greyish blue is a blue dulled with grey: the name Patrick Syme gave in 1821 to a mineralogist's smalt blue, later the color French soldiers wore into 1915, and the quiet blue of harbor skies.
Greyish brown is a plain descriptive name for a muted, earthy brown, and it is one of the most common colors in the paintings we have measured.
Greyish brownish olive is a muted, dark khaki, the library's double-modified variant of plain [[olive]], and it is one of the more common named colors in our archive.

Greyish green is a descriptive phrase, not a named color: a green with the brightness taken out, which the books reach for whenever they need to say that something looks dull, aged, military or quiet.
Greyish Teal is a soft, desaturated blue-green that our painting archive finds far more often than most crowd-survey colors, especially in Matisse and Klimt.
Greyish White is a color from the age of Werner's mineralogy: the eighth white on Syme's chart, defined as snow white with a touch of ash grey and illustrated with a kittiwake's feathers.
Guinea Hen is a dark olive grey that, in our data, only Maerz and Paul recorded, in 1930, and it is one of the most common colors in our entire painting archive.

Gull is an old English word for a shade of grey, now shown as a grayish olive; the books say little about it, but one nineteenth-century color chart took several of its whites and greys from gull feathers.
Gunmetal is the dark blue-grey of the alloy once used for cannon and gun parts, and it is now a standard word for a cool, dark grey.
Haematite Red is a dark, greyed brownish red, the color of iron ore and of the oldest red earth pigment.
Haematoxylin Violet is a moderate purple named for haematoxylin, the logwood-tree compound better known today as a laboratory stain than a painter's color.
Hair Brown is a grey-tinged, olive-leaning brown from the mineralogists' color lists of around 1800, defined then by a bird's head and a tin ore and later worn as a fashionable color.
Harbor blue is a muted, greenish [[blue]] whose name is undocumented: our sources record the color but not who named it or why.
Harvest Gold is a deep, saturated orange-yellow, the color of ripe grain and, to a generation, of 1970s kitchens.
Hathi Grey is a soft greenish grey that Ridgway standardized in 1912, and our archive finds a close match in roughly one painting in thirty-four.

Hay's Brown is a muted, warm brown that Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary names for a person, one of six Hay's colors in his book, and the only one the Inter-Society Color Council never repeated.

Hay's Green is a moderate, yellow-leaning green, one of six colors Robert Ridgway's 1912 dictionary names for a person called only Hay, and its closest color-graph match is another of the six, Ackermann's Green.

Hay's Lilac is a pale, dusty purple from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, and our archive's earliest match comes from just 43 years before Ridgway wrote the name down, closer than any of its five Hay's siblings, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin.
Hay's Maroon is a dark, greyed reddish brown from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, one of six colors he names for a person called only Hay.
Hay's Russet is a dark, reddish orange-brown from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, over-represented in paintings from Tibet and carried under a different name in Japan's own color lists.
Hazel is named for the hazelnut and the shrub it grows on; Paterson files it among the browns, while this screen swatch is a darker, greener gold.
Heat Wave is a vivid, fully saturated orange, a name from the modern lists of fashion and crayon shades, with no recorded author or date.

Heather grey is a dusty, purplish grey standardized by RAL in 1927, named after the small flowering shrub whose dried blooms turn this same muted purple-grey rather than the bright pink of its fresh flowers.
Heather pink is a vivid, slightly purplish pink standardized by RAL in 1927, named for the fresh flowers of the heather shrub rather than its faded, grey-toned Heather grey sibling.
Heather is the dusty purple of the moorland shrub's flowers, a muted mauve-grey that is more a texture than a single hue.
Heliotrope Grey is a pale, greyed purple named for the heliotrope flower, present in a small slice of our painting archive since the 1400s.
Heliotrope is a purple named for a flowering shrub, famous in late Victorian fashion for its bright combinations, its place in mourning dress and its appearance on stage in Oscar Wilde.
Honey yellow is a name from Werner's nineteenth-century colour list for minerals and animals, painted as a brownish gold by Patrick Syme in 1821.
Honeydew is a very pale green, a web-standard color name that shares a word with the melon, the sweet insect secretion, and an older pinkish tint.
Hooker's Green is a deep, cool watercolour green mixed from gamboge and Prussian blue or indigo, named for the English botanical artist who used it to paint leaves.
Hospital Green is a very light, slightly yellowish green from the 2010 xkcd color survey, named for an association with hospital walls and scrubs that our data does not trace further.
Hot Magenta is a fluorescent-bright pink-violet, the color of 1970s punk lettering and the Crayola fluorescent box.

Hot pink is an intensely saturated pink; a color Paterson calls particularly popular in the 1950s, close kin to Schiaparelli's shocking pink of 1937, and fixed on screens as one of the 140 X11 colors.
Hunter green is a dark, slightly yellowish green, the kind of color a dictionary file puts near Hooker's and Lincoln green.
Hyacinth blue is a deep purplish blue named for the flower, and its older echo, the biblical hyacinth blue, was a shade of cloth that stood beside scarlet and purple.
Hyacinth Red is the orange-red of the gem once called hyacinth, set down as number 83 in the English version of Werner's nomenclature of colors and used by Darwin on the Beagle.
Hyacinth Violet is a deep, reddish purple, named for the color of the flower in its purple form.
Hydrangea Pink is named for the flower, a soft pink with a hint of yellow, and for a plant whose color is famously unsteady.
Hydrangea Red is a muted, greyed red, the color of the flower heads when they take on a reddish tone.
Hydro is a muted grey-green from the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, first recorded in 1920, and none of the color books we hold explains the name.
Ice is a very pale cool tint, between blue and green: the color of light scattered inside snow and ice, and a name that painters, dyers and dictionaries have used in different ways.
Iceberg is a clear light blue that entered the color charts in the 1920s and 1930s; the books have almost nothing to say about it as a color.
Imperial Blue is a deep blue with a grand name, part of a small family of colors that borrowed "imperial" from the yellow of the Chinese court.
Imperial green is a nineteenth-century name for a copper-arsenic green related to emerald green, and today's swatch is a clean mid green far brighter than the dull pigment the trade manuals describe.
Imperial Jade is a strong, slightly blue-leaning green named for the most prized grade of jade, the gem that gives its name to one whole green family in our library.

Imperial purple was the shellfish dye of Rome and Byzantium, so costly that emperors fenced it with law; the muted blue-violet that carries its name on screen comes from a nineteenth-century mineralogist's color chart, not from the dye.
Imperial red is a strong, slightly bluish red whose name has pointed at an old court color, a pigment lake and the modern screen swatch.
Imperial Stone is a dark olive brown named for a landscape word, stone, and is among the most common named colors in our painting archive.

Imperial is a deep plum-violet named for imperial purple, the shellfish dye that Roman and Byzantine emperors kept for themselves; the word was later lent to blues, reds, yellows and greens that wanted the same majesty.
Inde blue is an old dictionary color name for a dark, greyish purple, despite the word blue in it.
Independence is a dark, dusty blue-violet whose name no color book explains.
Indian lake is an old name for a red lake pigment made from lac, the resin of an Asian scale insect; as a screen color it is a dull, greyish purplish red.
Indian red is an old pigment of finely ground iron oxide, a dark brownish red; the web color that borrows its name is a much lighter, pinker red.

Indian yellow is a deep, glowing golden yellow watercolor pigment that came from India in hard, foul-smelling balls, and its reputed source, the urine of mango-fed cows, is one of the best-known stories in the history of color, and one of the shakiest.
Indigo Blue is a mid greyish blue with three lives: the name of the dye's own colorant, a numbered entry in Werner's mineral color chart, and the everyday blue of denim.
Indigo dye is the deep, greyed blue made from the leaves of many plants, and the only major natural dye that works by being dissolved colorless and then turning blue in the air.

Indigo is two colors with one name: the deep, greyed blue of the oldest blue dye on earth, and the violet-blue band Newton squeezed into the rainbow. In Japan the dye is *ai*, and its blues have their own names.
Invisible green is a very dark green, named for how close it sits to black.
Iris Mauve is a pale, yellowish pink named for the iris flower, common in Indian paintings in our archive.
Iris purple is a vivid, reddish purple named for the iris flower, whose petals range far wider than any one swatch could show.
Iris is the blue-violet of the flower named for the Greek rainbow goddess; in the Middle Ages the same plant also gave painters a green, which is stranger than it sounds.
Irisglow is a pale, faintly purple grey that Maerz and Paul recorded in 1930, and no other system in our library repeats it.
Irresistible is a deep rose-crimson with a name that reads like a sales pitch; no book read uses it as a color, and its history is that of the shades around it.
Isabella Color is a dark, greyish yellow-tan, a swatch from Ridgway's atlases of 1886 and 1912.
Isabelline is a pale, faintly yellowish grey-white, an old name for the color of undyed linen and of pale dun animals, saddled with one of color history's most persistent bad jokes.
Ivory Brown is a dark, yellowish brown named for ivory, and it is the single most common named color in our painting archive.
Ivory is the off-white of an elephant's tusk, a color named for a material so prized that it gave us chessmen, bridal satin, a black pigment and a long trade in white gold.
Ivy green is a dark, muted olive green named for the leaves of ivy, and it is a surprisingly common color in painting.

Jacaranda Brown is a dark, grayish yellow-brown that Maerz and Paul recorded in 1930, and one of the most frequently matched colors in our entire painting archive, despite its name sitting in our Neutrals family rather than Browns.
Jade green is a green named for the stone, and Paterson's definition spans blue-green to yellowish green.
Jade is a green named for a stone, and the stone is really two unrelated minerals; the word came into English from a Spanish phrase for the flank, because the rock was once worn against kidney pain.
Japan Rose is a moderate, yellowish pink built from the word rose, over-represented in Indian paintings despite its name.
Japanese Carmine is a vivid, slightly brownish red, close kin to the dye word carmine, and the English name under which ColorHub files the Japanese color enji-iro.
Japonica is a dusty rose-mauve from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930, named with the Latin word for 'of Japan'.
Jasper Green is a muted, blue-leaning green named for jasper, the banded quartz usually associated with reds and browns rather than green.
Jasper Pink is a soft salmon-pink named for the stone jasper, and the English name ColorHub gives to a traditional Japanese color measured out by dye weight.
Jay Blue is a moderate, slightly greyed blue named for the jay bird, and it most often plays an accent color inside a painting.
Jet is a black gemstone made from fossilized wood, a hard, polishable lignite that Queen Victoria's long mourning turned into the color of grief and the livelihood of a Yorkshire fishing town.
Jouvence Blue is a dark greenish blue that Ridgway standardized in 1912, repeated by Maerz and Paul in 1930, and rare in our painting archive.
June Bud is a yellow-green named for the color of a leaf bud opening in early summer.
Jungle green is a modern name for a cool green; the name's definition and this swatch do not quite agree.
Kashmir is a dark, muted green named for the Himalayan valley; nothing in the books explains why, though the place is famous for shawls, saffron and sapphires.
Kelly green is the bright spring-grass green worn on St. Patrick's Day, a color named for an Irish surname and, by one account, only a century old.
Key Lime is a pale, creamy yellow-green named for the small, tart lime grown in the Florida Keys, though the survey that named it recorded two different greens under the same words.
Khaki Brown is a dark olive-brown, named from the dust-colored cloth of army uniforms.
Khaki Green is a moderate yellow-green that the ISCC-NBS system named directly in 1955, built on the family word khaki.
Khaki olive is a moderate, yellowish brown named for the olive, and it is among the most common named colors in our painting archive.
Khaki is a drab, dust-colored brownish yellow-green, named from an Indian-language word for dust, and the color that moved armies out of bright uniforms into ones meant to be hard to see.
Kiwi Green is a bright, yellow-leaning green named for the kiwifruit's flesh, brighter than our library's plain Kiwi entry for the same fruit.
Kobe is a deep brick-brown red from the color charts of the 1920s, and nothing in our books explains its name.
Kremlin is a deep blue-green from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of color, a name that has nothing to do with the walls it recalls.
Kronberg's Green is a muted, olive-leaning green from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color standards, and the books we hold do not say whom it was named for.
Laelia Pink is a moderate, purplish pink named for the orchid genus Laelia, rare in our painting archive and usually hidden there.
Lagoon blue is a saturated teal-blue named for the shallow, light-filled water of a lagoon, a vivid greenish blue by the ISCC-NBS classification.
Languid Lavender is a very pale purple named for the lavender plant, one of several near-duplicate names the ISCC-NBS system lists for roughly the same pale purple.
Lapis lazuli is the deep blue stone of Afghanistan, flecked with pyrite, that medieval painters turned into the most expensive pigment in Europe, ultramarine.
Lavender Blue is a pale, slightly violet blue named for the flower, and an old entry in the systems naturalists used to describe butterflies, flowers and stones.
Lavender Blush is an almost-white pink, one of the 140 named colors of the X11 set that web browsers adopted as CSS keywords.
Lavender grey is a pale, cool grey with a trace of purple, named for the color of lavender flowers.
Lavender Pink is a bright, warm purple-pink that sits between its two namesakes, closer to orchid than to either lavender or pink alone.
Lavender violet is an xkcd survey name that pairs the paler flower color lavender with the stronger, more saturated violet.
Lavender is the pale bluish purple of lavender flowers, a color word English has used since the early 1700s, and a name that has been pinned to several quite different swatches since.
Leaf green is the yellowish green of young leaves, and also, in the pigment trade, an old name for a durable pale green made from chromium.
Leaf is a fresh, strong yellow-green, the color a young leaf shows against the light; the same word in older color lists names the brown of a dead one.
Leather is the color of tanned hide, a mid orange-brown named for a material that has been dyed nearly every other color, from Egyptian canopies stained blue to Charlemagne's scarlet shoes.
Leek green is the greyed, yellowish green of the leek's leaf; the Greeks built a word for green on it, Davy named chlorine for it, and Werner's mineral chart made it number 48.
Leghorn is the pale yellow of bleached straw, named for the Italian port that gave its name to a famous straw hat.
Seafoam Green is a pale yellow-beige that Maerz and Paul trace to 1892, sharing a name but no real kinship with the bright green Seafoam.
Lemon yellow is a bright, cool yellow named for the fruit, and as a paint it was a family of nineteenth-century chromium and cadmium pigments sold under one name.
Lettuce green is a soft yellowish green named for lettuce leaves, with a long record in color dictionaries.
Levant red is an alternative name for Turkey red, a brilliant alizarin red dye used in Britain from 1785 into the 1930s.
Liberty Blue is a dark, slightly purplish blue first recorded in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, named for the word liberty for reasons no source consulted here explains.
Liberty is a mid blue-violet that has a place in three color lists and in none of the color books; its name has no documented story, while the idea it names has been given red, green, buff and blue.
Lichen green is a very pale, cool green, named for the whitish green of lichen.
Light Blue Grey is a light shade of [[blue-grey|blue-grey]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.
Light blue is the plain name for a pale blue, and it points at a different swatch in almost every standard; its real history is in who could wear it, what it cost to dye, and how it behaves at dusk.
Light brown is a plain description rather than a historic color name, and old color dictionaries use it as a gloss for dozens of earthy names from ochre to biscuit.
Light Brownish Drab is a muted reddish tan from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, close enough to Pale Taupe and Warm Grey that the three are hard to tell apart on screen.
Light Brownish Vinaceous is a pale, dusty pink from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, sitting closer to Silver Pink than to any true brown.
Light Cadmium is a warm, slightly dull gold, named after cadmium yellow light, the pale end of the cadmium sulfide pigments.
Vinaceous-Cinnamon is a warm, wine-tinged orange-brown, a deeper member of Robert Ridgway's "vinaceous" family carried over from his 1886 bird-and-mammal nomenclature.
Light Columbia Blue is a pale, slightly grey sky blue, the library's lightened variant of [[columbia-blue]], the shade long tied to Columbia University's athletic color.
Light Congo Pink is a soft apricot pink from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, a lighter sibling of the deeper Congo Pink rather than a color with its own separate history.
Light coral is a web color, a soft pinkish red from the X11 set, defined by its hex code rather than a long history.
Light Cornflower Blue is a very light blue named for the cornflower, close enough to Sky Blue in our library that the two are almost interchangeable.
Light Cyan is a very pale aqua tint, a CSS and X11 keyword whose parent word, cyan, is a primary of printing.
Light Danube Green is a muted, slightly blue-leaning green named for the Danube, the river that crosses central and southeastern Europe, and recorded as a color standard since at least 1912.

Light Drab is a pale yellowish tan from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, one of the closest matches between Ridgway's original reading and the 1955 dictionary that filed it, and one of the most common tones in our painting archive.
Light Fluorite Green is a pale, yellow-leaning green named for fluorite, the mineral whose green variety can glow under ultraviolet light.
Light Forest Green is a mid, leafy green from the 2010 xkcd color survey, the lighter counterpart to Dark Forest Green, both built as modifiers on the same base name.
Light Grape Green is a muted, greyish yellow-green named for the grape, plotted by Ridgway in 1912 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a moderate yellow green.

Light Green is the web's pale, fresh green, one of the X11 colors; the words "light green" are far older than the screen, and across the books they mark a green that is young, cheerful and easy on the eye.
Light Grey Green is a descriptive name for a pale, softly greyed spring green, and it has been in color charts since 1912.
Light Grey is the pale neutral that web designers know as `lightgrey`, and a plain descriptive name that the books use for mourning cloth, Vermeer's walls and overcast skies.
Light Hortense Violet is a bright pink-violet named for hortense, the French word for hydrangea, and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a brilliant purple.
Light Hyssop Violet is a pale, greyed violet named for the herb hyssop, recorded by Ridgway in 1912 and filed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 among ten different names for the same pale-violet block.

Light Ivory is a pale, warm beige standardized by the German RAL paint system in 1927 and later carried into the American ISCC-NBS color dictionary, grammatically a lighter version of Ivory rather than its own invention.
Light Jasper Red is a bright, coral-leaning pink named for jasper, close enough to our library's Rose Doree to be a near-duplicate.
Light Khaki is a pale, yellow-green khaki, built from the modifier "light" rather than drawn from any dated military or dye source.
Light King's Blue is a soft, greyed sky blue from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, a lightened version of the pigment name King's Blue rather than a blue with its own separate history.
Light Lavender is a very pale violet, a lightened lavender, and as a painted color it is almost absent from the museum record.
Light Light Green is a pale, almost washed-out mint from the 2010 xkcd color survey, named by doubling the modifier *light* on the plain word *green* rather than borrowing a new word.
Light Lime is a pale yellow-green built by adding the modifier light to lime, recorded in both the 1955 ISCC-NBS system and the 2010 xkcd color survey.
Light Mallow Purple is a bright pink-purple named for the mallow flower, recorded by Ridgway in 1912 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a deep purplish pink.
Light Mint is a very pale yellowish green recorded only in the 2010 xkcd color survey, close enough to two other surveyed names to call them near-duplicates.
Light Mouse Grey is a warm, brownish grey, the library's lightened variant of [[mouse-grey]], and our archive finds it in roughly one painting in ten.
Light Olive is a descriptive name for a pale olive, and the books show it in an old color-chart skin description and as part of a paint name.
Light Orange-Yellow is a bright, warm yellow from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, filed by our library as a lighter child of Light Orange rather than a color with its own separate naming history.
Light orange is a descriptive name for a pale, warm orange; the books mostly use it as a plain description rather than a named color.
Light orchid is a very pale, pink-leaning purple, a tint of orchid carried in the ISCC-NBS 1955 standard as well as the 2010 xkcd survey.
Light Pea Green is a vivid yellow-green named for the pea, submitted to the crowdsourced XKCD color survey in 2010 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system as a brilliant yellow green.
Light Periwinkle is a pale greyish blue-violet that four separate systems have recorded since 1912, and one of our museum archive's more common named colors.
Light Pink is the web's name for a pale, slightly warm pink, one of the 140 colors in the X11 set and later in CSS, with the hex code #FFB6C1.
Light Plum is a muted reddish purple recorded only in the 2010 xkcd color survey, with ten alternate names clustered around the same hue in our library.
Light Purplish Vinaceous is a pale, dusty mauve-pink from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, rarer in our painting archive than most of the colors in this group.
Light Red is a painter's name for the brownish red made by burning yellow ochre, and also a plain description of a bright red; the screen swatch here is the second, not the first.
Light Sage is a pale yellowish green recorded only in the 2010 xkcd color survey, close enough to two ISCC-NBS names to count as near-duplicates.
Light salmon is a web color, a soft pinkish orange from the X11 set named as a lighter salmon.
Light sea green is a web color, a cool teal-green from the X11 set, that is actually fairly dark for a name that says light.
Light Seafoam is a bright, very pale green recorded only in the 2010 xkcd color survey, and its own library entry marks it as close kin to Light Mint.
Light Slate Grey is a cool, bluish grey that is a named color in CSS, with the spelling gray or grey both accepted in the web names.
Light Tan is a pale cream-yellow on screens, much lighter than the leather tan its name suggests, and it has a family of older names.
Light Teal is a pale green recorded in Wikipedia's color lists and the 2010 xkcd survey, with nine near-duplicate names clustered in one ISCC-NBS block.
Light Violet-Grey is a near-neutral medium grey, filed by Ridgway in 1912 under the violet family though its measured chroma is almost zero.
Light Violet is a soft blue-violet whose name has meant different colors on different charts; on one survey it is a pale pink-lilac instead.
Light yellow is a descriptive name for a very pale yellow, best known today as an entry in the web's X11 color list, and in older books a loose label for pale yellow pigments, dyes and fabrics.
Lighter Green is a bright yellow-green recorded in Wikipedia's color lists and the 2010 xkcd survey, built from the comparative lighter rather than the usual light.
Lightish Blue is a vivid mid-blue recorded in Wikipedia's color lists, the 2010 xkcd survey and, by Wikipedia's account, Crayola, built from the hedging modifier lightish.
Lightish Red is a bright pink-red recorded in Wikipedia's color lists and the 2010 xkcd survey, with two near-duplicate names only a little over a unit away.
Lilac-Grey is a pale, warm-leaning light grey with only a whisper of violet, a name carried over from Ridgway's color nomenclature.
Lilac is the pale, slightly pinkish purple of the lilac blossom, a word with a dark blue ancestor that was the common-speech name for the first mass-market purple dye.
Lily green is a pale yellow-green with two lives: a rarely used name in color dictionaries, and a medieval flower pigment that probably came from iris, not lilies.
Lime green is a vivid, slightly yellowish green; on the web it is X11's #32CD32, while the older paint of the same name was a copper-and-arsenic green thinned with a white calcium filler.
Lime Yellow is a vivid, green-leaning yellow, bright enough to sit on the border between yellow and green.
Lime is the yellowish green of the lime fruit, and the same word names the white caustic mineral that coated walls, set fresco and sat in dye vats for centuries.
Linen grey is a warm, dusty neutral from the Ridgway and ISCC-NBS naming lineage, so close to pink in the 1955 dictionary's own categories that it was filed as a shade of brownish pink, not grey.
Linen is the pale, faintly pink off-white of the X11 color set, named for cloth woven from flax, the oldest textile known, whose natural color is greyer and browner than its name suggests.
Lint is a muted, yellowish tan from the fashion color cards of the early twentieth century.
Lion is a pale sandy yellow, named for the coat of the animal and recorded as a color name by Maerz and Paul in 1930.
Lipstick Red is a strong, slightly blue red, a name that reads as ordinary language but has no documented origin.
Lipstick is a deep pink-red named for a cosmetic, and the cosmetic's own reds have come from cinnabar, from cochineal insects and from the laboratory.
Litho Purple is a dusty, grayed purple named from the Greek root for stone, one of a scattered set of color words built on *litho-*.
Liver Brown is a dark, slightly reddish brown that comes straight out of the mineralogists' colour list, where it was defined as a recipe: chestnut brown darkened with a little black and olive green.
Liver is a dark, greyed reddish brown named for the organ, a color that ancient doctors used to describe a red earth and eighteenth-century naturalists used to rank browns.
Livid Violet is a dark, greyed purple recorded by Ridgway in 1912 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a light grayish red.
Log Cabin is a near-neutral dark grey-brown from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, sitting in a crowded cluster of dark neutrals that includes Plum Grey and Greyish Black.
Long Beach is a light yellowish tan from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, and the single most common color matched in our entire painting archive.
Lumiere Blue is a pale grey-green teal on screens, and its name echoes an obscure artificial pigment, bleu lumière, listed in 1901.
Lumiere Green is a pale yellow-green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, rare in our painting archive but matched in a Dutch still life painted 270 years before the name existed.
Lupine is a soft, slightly greyed blue named for the lupine flower, recorded by the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1930 with a first use in 1922.
Macaroni and Cheese is a warm, pale orange named for the baked pasta dish, recorded by both Wikipedia and the 2010 xkcd color survey as the same hue.
Madder Blue is a greyish violet-blue named in Ridgway's atlas, and a puzzle: madder gives reds, and our sources do not say why a blue carries its name.
Madder brown is a reddish brown named for the madder root: a nineteenth-century artist's pigment made by gently heating madder lake until it turned from red to brown.
Madder lake is the painter's form of the madder root: its red dye fixed on a colorless base, sold in grades from deep carmine to pale rose, loved for its glow and blamed for its fading.
Madder Violet is a deep, reddish purple named for the dye plant that gives madder red, and a color that old dyers and color chartmakers recognized as one of madder's side effects.
Madder is the red of a root: probably the oldest dye people ever made, the secret behind Turkey red and rose madder, and the first natural dye ever rebuilt in a laboratory.

Magenta is the red-purple of the first magenta dye, a coal-tar color made in France in 1858 or 1859 and named for a battle in Italy; on screens and in printing it is now the pure pink-purple where red and blue light meet.
Mahogany Brown is a very dark reddish brown named for polished mahogany wood, and it is also the paint standard RAL 8016.
Mahogany Red is a warm red-brown named for the hardwood, and Maerz and Paul's dictionary dates it to 1843.
Mahogany is the dark reddish brown of polished mahogany wood, a name that furniture makers, dyers and painters' colormen all borrowed.
Maize Yellow is a pale, creamy yellow named for corn, carried in our library from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas and still echoed in RAL's industrial paint list.
Maize is a bright, warm yellow named for the ripe kernels of the American grain that English calls corn.
Majorelle Blue is a vivid blue-violet named for the French painter Jacques Majorelle, who painted the walls and pergolas of his Marrakech garden in this color during the 1920s and 1930s.

Malachite green is the green of the copper mineral malachite, which painters ground into pigment for thousands of years; the same name was later given to a coal-tar dye, so it points at several different materials.
Malachite is a banded green copper mineral, ground as a pigment since ancient Egypt and named for the mallow leaf, that gave its name to a vivid green on screens and to a family of later greens.
Mallow Pink is a soft purplish pink named for the mallow flower, recorded by the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1930 with a first use in 1912.
Mallow Red is a muted, purplish crimson named for the mallow flower, close kin to mauve.
Manatee is a cool, purplish grey named for the skin of the aquatic mammal, a muted color meant to evoke a creature often called a sea cow.
Mandarin Orange is a deep, reddish orange named for the fruit; a dictionary calls the name a reddish yellow, and the exact tone has drifted.
Mandarin is a vivid reddish orange named for the mandarin fruit, a word that also names Chinese officials, a garnet and a style of robe, and the books do not agree on which exact orange it is.
Manganese Violet is a muted red-violet that takes its name from a nineteenth-century artists' pigment, introduced in 1868 as a safer replacement for cobalt violet.
Manila is a light yellowish brown, a color name Maerz and Paul date to 1892 and shared with the Philippine capital.
Mantis is a fresh, light leaf green; the books say nothing about it as a color, but they have a lot to say about the animals that share the name.
Maple is an orangey-yellow, and the tree behind the name gives painters, violin makers and dyers three very different stories.
Marguerite Yellow is a pale, buttery yellow first plated by Ridgway in 1912, and so close to a color Wikipedia lists as Lemon Meringue that the two amount to the same paint.
Marie Antoinette is a dusty pink-brown named for the last queen of the old French monarchy; the name entered the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1926, long after her death.

Marigold is the warm orange-yellow of the garden flower, a color that naturalists once used as a standard for orange, that a pigment maker used as a shade name, and that got a Nuremberg saffron dealer burned for fraud in 1444, according to one book.
Marine Blue is a dark, slightly greenish blue of the sea; the one dictionary that defines it ties it to a military uniform.
Marine is a very dark blue, close to navy, whose name is the French bleu marine in English clothes; its best-documented career is as the color that replaced black in uniforms.
Maroon is a dark brownish red, named from the French word for the chestnut, and it began as a brown before it became a red.
Mars orange is a reddish orange paint made synthetically from iron oxide, one of a family of eighteenth-century pigments named for the alchemists' planet-metal Mars.
Mars is a warm orange named for the planet, one of a family of Mars pigments (Mars yellow, Mars red, Mars black) made from synthetic iron oxide rather than natural earths.
Marsh Rose is a muted, dusty red-brown named for the rose, recorded by the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1930 with a first use in 1927.
Mascot is a very dark navy blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and the reason for its name is undocumented.
Massicot is a yellow oxide of lead, one of the oldest painters' yellows, and a pale, creamy one on screen.
Mathews' Purple is a mid-toned, reddish purple from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color standards, and no book we hold records whom it honors.
Mauve Blush is a warm, dusty tan, filed under the mauve family though it reads as brown rather than purple, recorded by the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1930 with a first use in 1928.
Mauve brown is the English name our data gives to Hatobanezumi, a traditional Japanese color whose name translates as "dove feather grey."
Mauve grey is a muted, greyed violet-pink, one of several modifiers built on the flower name [[mauve]], first charted by Ridgway in 1912 and picked up again in the ISCC-NBS system in 1955.

Mauve rose is a dusty, greyish pink-purple on the warmer side of the [[mauve]] family, dated to Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature and confirmed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a close match to its own "light grayish purplish red" block.

Mauve Taupe is a dusty, muted rose-brown on the dark side of the [[mauve]] family, dated by Maerz and Paul to about 1925 and confirmed in 1955 by the ISCC-NBS system, which lists it a close 1.1 units from its own "dark reddish gray" block.
Mauve is the French name of the mallow flower, borrowed for a soft greyish purple; in 1856 an 18-year-old chemist made a coal-tar dye that took the name and turned it into a craze.
Mauvette is a very pale, pinkish lilac, a diminutive cousin of mauve.
May Green is a mid, slightly yellowish green, the name RAL gave to its standard color 6017, and one that a pigment reference files as a rare variant name for emerald green.
Mayflower is a deep pink named for the trailing spring flower rather than the ship, first recorded by Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color.
Mazarine Blue is an old name for a rich blue, possibly honoring a French cardinal; the modern swatch is much lighter than the word suggests.
Meadow Violet is a deep, saturated reddish purple built on the landscape word *meadow*, dated by Maerz and Paul to 1928 and absent from our own painting archive entirely.
Meadow is a dark, slightly yellowish green named for hay-and-grass country, a word that mineralogists, pigment makers and painters each used in their own way.
Meadowgrass is a dark, yellowish green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, close enough to [[hunter-green|Hunter Green]] that the two likely come from the same part of the chart.
Medici Blue is a greyed, muted blue-green from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color standards, and no book we hold confirms whether the name points to the Florentine family or to someone else entirely.
Medium Aquamarine is a soft sea-green from the named colors of the web.
Medium Blue is a pure, saturated blue, one of the named colors of the web.
Medium Orchid is a bright, blue-leaning violet-pink, one of the named colors of the web.
Medium Pink is a saturated, slightly bluish pink, a plain descriptive name that a 2010 online color survey put on the map and that no color book treats as a color of its own.
Medium Purple is a soft, blue-leaning purple from the named colors of the web.
Medium Slate Blue is a bright, electric blue-violet that exists as a color name because it sits in the X11 color list and, from there, in the CSS color keywords.
Medium Turquoise is a clear blue-green from the X11 and CSS color lists, a neighbor of turquoise.
Melon is a pale, warm pink with a touch of orange, named for the flesh of a ripe fruit and recorded as a color name since at least 1892.
Merlot is a very dark purplish red named for the red wine grape, recorded in the 2010 xkcd color survey and also known in our library as Claret Violet.
Metallic Blue is a grayish steel blue named by an online color survey, borrowing the vocabulary of car paint for a color that is flat on a screen.
Metallic Gold is a warm yellow, a flat screen stand-in for the look of the metal itself.

Metallic Green is a dark olive from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; despite the name, the swatch is closer to olive brown than to green, and the copper greens that painters called metallic are a different thing.
Michigan is a deep teal green-blue from the Maerz and Paul dictionary; the books say nothing about why it carries a state's name.
Microcline Green is a very pale green named for microcline, a feldspar mineral whose green variety is better known by its own name, amazonite.
Middle grey is the grey halfway between black and white, a reference that painters and designers use to judge every other color.

Midnight blue is the blue of the sky at its darkest, a deep violet-leaning navy that Paterson's dictionary says was apparently the correct shade for men's evening dress, before it became a crayon, a screen color and a name for oxidized indigo.
Midnight Green is a near-black teal, a landscape-and-time-of-day compound that our library files as the darkest member of the midnight family of names.

Midnight navy is a near-black blue that compounds two familiar color words, midnight and navy, the second of them pointing to naval uniform blue rather than any single document our library records a date for.
Midnight Purple is a near-black purple from a 2010 online color survey, named for the dark of night and barely distinguishable on screen from Deep Purple.
Midnight is the color of the sky at its darkest, a name that books use for deep indigo blues, and the swatch here is a near-black navy that few painters ever needed.
Mikado Brown is a light, tan-leaning brown from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, named for the Japanese imperial title rather than for any dye or wood.
Mikado Orange is a strong, warm orange plated twice by Ridgway in 1912 and echoed in RAL's industrial list, sharing its name but not its hue with the duller [[mikado-brown|Mikado Brown]].
Military Green is a dull, yellowish olive from a 2010 crowd color survey, close enough to uniform drab that the name reads as obvious even though no army ever registered it.
Milk Chocolate is a warm mid-brown named for the candy bar, and one of the most common colors in our painting archive even though chocolate itself reached Europe only in the 1500s.
Mineral green is a name that colourmen attached to many different green pigments, mostly copper compounds, so it points to a family of recipes and a trade habit more than to one substance.
Mineral Red is a muted brownish red from Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature, a descriptive name rather than the record of a single pigment.
Ming is a deep, greyed greenish-blue named for the Chinese dynasty and its porcelain, though the porcelain's famous blue was cobalt, a different and more violet color.
Mint Cream is a near-white with the faintest green tint, a screen color from the X11 and CSS lists.
Mint leaf is a clear, light yellowish green dated to Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature, and despite the garden-herb name it is one of the rarest colors in our painting archive.
Mint Turquoise is a muted blue-green standardized as RAL 6033, a paint color shared with the stone that gives turquoise its name.
Mint is the pale, cool green of the herb's leaves, a pastel that has come to mean freshness and cleanliness.
Minty Green is a bright, yellowish spring green listed in the CSS and X11 color sets, and a word for color that goes back to 1766 even though this exact hex is recent.
Misty Rose is a very pale pink, a screen color from the X11 and CSS lists.
Mocha is a warm, mid-toned coffee brown named for the drink; Paterson's definition is darker than the swatch most people mean.
Mole brown is a muted, warm grey-brown named for the animal's coat, listed by Ridgway in 1912 and matched in our own graph to the Japanese traditional grey Sunezumi, "plain mouse."
Mona Lisa is a light, warm pink on web color lists; the name apparently borrows Leonardo's portrait, though the pink it suggests is the one the painting lost.
Monkey Skin is a light reddish brown dated by Maerz and Paul to 1927, and our graph's nearest named neighbor for it, Reddish Grey, differs mainly by being a touch redder.
Montpellier green is a name for verdigris, the green made from copper, taken from the French city that was an important verdigris-making center for several centuries.
Morocco Red is a dark reddish brown named for Morocco, the North African country whose goatskin leather, tanned and dyed this color, gave English the word morocco for fine bookbinding leather.

Morocco is the color of a leather, a deep brown in the library but a brick red in the one glossary that explains the word, and it is named for a country the color books mostly visit for other reasons.
Moss green is a muted yellowish green named for the plant, and the name has also been used for a pigment whose identity the books cannot agree on.
Moss Grey is a muted greenish grey, a color defined by the old RAL system and the ISCC-NBS names.
Moss olive is an xkcd survey name pairing two plant colors, the green of woodland moss and the duller yellow-green of olive.

Moss is the yellowish, softly greyed green of the plant that carpets stones and trees, a color word that dictionaries define by the plant and paint catalogues borrowed for several different mixed greens.
Mossy Green is a medium, yellowish green that names the color of moss, and the same words turn up in recipes for making a dark green out of old verdigris.
Mosul is a moderate yellowish brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the Iraqi city that was once a market for textiles and dye materials.

Motmot Green is a muted yellowish green named for the motmot, a Central and South American bird with iridescent green-backed plumage, charted by Ridgway in 1912 and confirmed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955.
Mountain green is a pale grey-green from Syme's 1821 color nomenclature, which shares its name with an older pigment word for green copper minerals such as malachite.
Mountbatten pink is a dull, greyed mauve-pink that a British naval officer adopted as ship camouflage in the early Second World War; its fame rests on one tale of a lucky cruiser.
MSU Green is a very dark, slightly blue green used as a school color, its initials standing for a state university rather than any pigment or dye.
Mud Green is a dark, yellow-leaning olive named for wet earth, close enough to Brownish Green that the library files the two as near-duplicates.
Mud is the color of wet soil, a name that has carried a faint insult for painters and a good deal of practical use for dyers and soldiers.
Muddy Brown is a dull, yellow-leaning brown from a 2010 crowd color survey, a dirtier-looking neighbor of Milk Chocolate and Mustard on screen.
Muddy Green is a dull, dark olive from a 2010 crowd color survey, close enough to Military Green that most eyes would call them the same color.
Mulberry is named for the fruit of the mulberry tree, and for centuries it meant a dark purplish red; on a screen today it is a brighter, pinker magenta.

Mushroom brown is a light, grayish reddish brown charted by Ridgway in 1912 and matched closely, 2.1 units, by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955, a block that at least ten other twentieth-century trade names also claimed.
Mushroom is a pale greyish brown with a warm pink cast, named plainly for the vegetable.
Musk is a dark, warm brown named for the strong-smelling secretion of the male musk deer, and the dictionaries date the color name to 1654.
Mustard Brown is a deep, brownish yellow named for prepared mustard, recorded in color charts by the 1920s.
Mustard Green is a sharp, acid yellow-green named for the condiment, almost identical on screen to Acid Green and rare in our painting archive.
Mustard yellow is the deep, slightly warm yellow of the table condiment, a name that grew out of the shorter word mustard.
Mustard is the deep yellow of the condiment, a color that eighteenth-century France briefly adored and Europeans have mostly distrusted since.
Myrtle Green is a dark bluish green named for the leaf of the myrtle shrub, recorded in color charts since Ridgway's 1886 nomenclature.
Naiad is a soft, light green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the water nymphs of Greek myth.
Napoleon Blue is a deep, violet-leaning blue that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to 1850, nearly thirty years after the emperor it is named for died.
Natural is a pale, warm tan from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, a name so generic it describes almost any unbleached or undyed fiber rather than one specific thing.
Navy Green is a dark, strong olive named after the institution rather than a place, and recorded by Maerz and Paul as early as about 1904, decades before the crowd survey that named this exact hex.
Navy is a dark, slightly greyed blue named for naval uniforms, which were dyed with indigo; in the twentieth century it replaced black as the color of work uniforms and men's suits.
Near black is a black with a trace of color in it, which is how some painters, from Gauguin on, made their darkest darks.
Neon Blue is a vivid, electric blue whose earliest record in our data is not the modern word *neon* at all but a butterfly's wing in Werner's 1821 Nomenclature of Colours.
Neon Red is an extremely saturated red, named for the glow of a neon tube, and a good example of a color no tube of paint and no flat screen swatch can fully reproduce.
Neuwieder Green is a light, yellowish green that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to around 1850, likely after the German town of Neuwied, known historically for its dye and chemical works.
Neva Green is a muted yellow-green named for the Neva, the short, fast river that carries Lake Ladoga's water through Saint Petersburg to the Gulf of Finland.
New Hay is a dark, grayish olive green dated by Maerz and Paul to 1892, a name that sounds like pale cut grass but names a shadowed olive instead.
New York Pink is a dusty, brownish pink from Wikipedia's color lists, named for the city rather than any pigment or dye.
Newport is a deep, muted blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, close enough to [[denim|Denim]] that painted denim is its single strongest match in our archive.
Niagara Green is a pale, greyed blue-green named for Niagara Falls, the waterfalls on the border of Canada and the United States, and recorded as a color standard since 1912.
Nickel Green is a grayish green named for the metal, close enough to two other Ridgway plate colors that our library flags them as near-duplicates.
